en: Thus have I heard: Majjhima Nikāya 111, the Anupada Sutta.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, Sāriputta is wise;”
"Bhikkhus, Sāriputta has great wisdom;
bhikkhus, Sāriputta has expansive wisdom;
bhikkhus, Sāriputta has joyful wisdom."
Monks, Sāriputta has swift wisdom;
monks, Sāriputta has sharp wisdom;
monks, Sāriputta has penetrative wisdom.
“Monks, Sāriputta practiced insight into phenomena according to their sequence for half a month.
This, monks, was Sāriputta’s insight into phenomena according to their sequence:

Here, monks, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, Sāriputta entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.”
And those states that exist in the first jhāna— namely, applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, pleasure,
and one-pointedness of mind; contact, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness, desire, resolve, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and attention—
these states are defined by him one by one as they arise.
Those phenomena arise for him known, they persist known, and they pass away known.
He understands thus:
"So it is that these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they vanish."
Thus, with respect to those phenomena, being without approach, without departure, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, he dwells with a mind that has transcended all limits.
He understands: "There is a further escape.
Through frequent cultivation of that, there truly exists for him [the realization of] its existence.

Furthermore, monks, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, Sāriputta enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and is born of concentration, consisting of rapture and happiness.
And as for those states in the second jhāna—internal tranquility, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind;
contact, feeling, perception, volition, and mind; desire, resolve, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and attention—all these are present in him.
Phenomena are defined in successive stages.
Those phenomena arise for him known, they persist known, and they pass away known.
He understands thus:
‘Thus indeed these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they vanish.
Toward those phenomena, he dwells without approach, without departure, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, with a mind that has transcended all boundaries.
He understands: “There is a further escape.”
Through the frequent cultivation of that, there is indeed its presence.
Furthermore, monks, through the fading away of rapture, Sāriputta dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body—of which the Noble Ones declare: “He who is equanimous and mindful dwells happily.”
“He dwells in happiness” means that he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

As for the phenomena present in the third jhāna—namely, happiness, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and one-pointedness of mind; contact, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness, desire, resolve, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and attention—these phenomena are defined by him one by one.
These phenomena are known by him as they arise, known as they persist, and known as they pass away.
Thus he understands:
"Indeed, these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they vanish.
Toward those phenomena, he dwells without attraction, without repulsion, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, with a mind for which the boundaries of the world have been broken down.
Thus he understands: "There is a further escape.
Through frequent practice of that, there is indeed for him the conviction that it exists.
Furthermore, monks, Sāriputta—through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous [cessation of elation and depression]—
With the subsiding of both joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
And as for those phenomena present in the fourth jhāna— equanimity, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and mental composure due to tranquility— [he understands them as they really are].

Purity of mindfulness and one-pointedness of mind; contact, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness, desire, resolve, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and attention—these phenomena are defined by him in successive order.
These phenomena arise known to him, they persist known, and they pass away known.
Thus he understands:
"Indeed, these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they vanish.
Toward those phenomena, he dwells without attraction, without repulsion, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, with a mind for which the boundaries of the world have been transcended.
Thus he understands: "There is a further escape.
Through frequent practice of that, there is indeed for him the conviction that it exists.

Furthermore, monks, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] "space is infinite," Sāriputta enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
And as for those phenomena in the base of infinite space— the perception of the base of infinite space, one-pointedness of mind, contact, feeling, perception, volition,
consciousness, desire, resolve, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and attention—
these phenomena are defined by him one by one in successive order.
Those phenomena arise for him known, they persist known, and they pass away known.
He understands thus:
"Indeed, these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they vanish."
Thus, with respect to those phenomena, being without approach, without departure, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, he dwells with a mind that has transcended all limits.
He understands: "There is a further escape.
Through repeated cultivation of this, there truly comes to be for him [the realization of] its existence.
Furthermore, monks, Sāriputta, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving: "Consciousness is infinite.
And as for those phenomena in the base of infinite consciousness—the perception of the base of infinite consciousness and one-pointedness of mind;
contact, feeling, perception, volition, mind, desire, resolve, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and attention—these phenomena are present in him.
They are established without clinging.
Those phenomena arise for him known, they persist known, and they pass away known.
He understands thus:
‘Thus indeed these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they pass away.
Toward those phenomena, he dwells without approach, without retreat, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, with a mind that has transcended all boundaries.
He understands: “There is a further escape.”
Through frequent practice of that, there is indeed the existence of it.
Furthermore, monks, Sāriputta, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, enters and dwells in the base of nothingness, [perceiving] "there is nothing.
And as for those phenomena in the base of nothingness—the perception of the base of nothingness and one-pointedness of mind, contact, feeling...
Perception, volition, consciousness, desire, resolve, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and attention—
these states are defined by him one after another.
These states arise known to him, they persist known, and they pass away known.
Thus he understands:
"Indeed, these phenomena, having not existed, come into being; having existed, they pass away.
Toward those phenomena, he dwells without attraction, without repulsion, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, with a mind for which the boundaries of the world have been removed.
Thus he understands: "There is a further escape.
Through frequent practice of that, it truly exists for him.
Furthermore, monks, Sāriputta, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus, mindful, he emerges from that attainment.
Having emerged from that attainment while remaining mindful, he contemplates those states that have passed away, ceased, and changed, thinking:
"Indeed, these states, having not been, come to be; having been, they vanish."
Thus, regarding those phenomena, he dwells with a mind that is without approach, without departure, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, having transcended all boundaries.
He understands: "There is a further escape. Through the frequent cultivation of that understanding, there truly exists for him [the realization of that escape].

Furthermore, bhikkhus, Sāriputta, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. Having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
He emerges mindfully from that attainment.
Having emerged mindfully from that attainment, he contemplates those states that are past, ceased, and changed:
‘Thus indeed these phenomena, having not existed, come into being; having existed, they vanish.
Toward those phenomena, he dwells without approach, without departure, undependent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, with a mind for which the boundaries of perception have been transcended.
He understands: “There is no further escape beyond this.”
"There is no further cultivation of that," he thinks.
Monks, if one were speaking rightly, it would be said of him:
"He has reached mastery, he has reached perfection in noble virtue; he has reached mastery, he has reached perfection in noble concentration."
‘He has attained mastery, he has reached perfection in noble wisdom;
he has attained mastery, he has reached perfection in noble liberation’—it is of Sāriputta alone that one could rightly say:

‘He has attained mastery, he has reached perfection in noble virtue; he has attained mastery, he has reached perfection in noble concentration; he has attained mastery, he has reached perfection in noble wisdom; he has attained mastery, he has reached perfection in noble liberation.’”
“Monks, if one were speaking rightly, saying:

‘A son of the Blessed One, born from his breast, born from his mouth, born of the Dhamma, fashioned by the Dhamma, an heir to the Dhamma, not an heir to material things,’ it is of Sāriputta alone that one would rightly say this:
‘A son of the Blessed One, born from his breast, born from his mouth, born of the Dhamma, fashioned by the Dhamma, an heir to the Dhamma, not an heir to material things.’”
“Monks, Sāriputta correctly continues to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Tathāgata.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Elated, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Discourse on the Footprint is finished; the first.
